subject: selective
title: Verbal reasoning · Test 1
summary: A 40-question, 30-minute practice test for the selective entry Verbal reasoning section: analogies, odd one out, word meanings, letter series and codes, hidden words and logic.
body:
This practice test covers the Verbal reasoning section of the Victorian selective entry test: analogies, odd one out, synonyms and antonyms, letter series and codes, hidden words and word building, and logical deduction.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** 30 minutes for 40 questions — about 45 seconds each.
- **Conditions:** no notes, no dictionary and no calculator. Use scrap paper for letter series and logic puzzles.
- **Pacing:** if a question takes more than a minute, choose your best guess and move on. Answer every question — a guess gives you a chance, a blank gives you none.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, read its hints and go back to the lesson it came from. Then try another Verbal reasoning test — each one has different questions.

questions.prompt: Complete the analogy: puppy is to dog as kitten is to ___.
questions.explanation: A puppy is a young dog, so a kitten is a young cat. Milk is what a kitten drinks, not what it grows into.
steps: Say the first pair as a sentence: a puppy is a young dog.
Use the same sentence for the second pair: a kitten is a young cat — so the answer is cat.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a kitten might chase a mouse, but that is not the link. A puppy grows up into a dog — what does a kitten grow up into?
mistakes.C: Step 2: kittens drink milk, but the first pair is 'young animal → adult animal'. Use that same link.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you used a dog idea (where a dog sleeps). Test the 'young → adult' link on the kitten instead.

questions.prompt: Complete the analogy: glove is to hand as sock is to ___.
questions.explanation: A glove covers a hand, and a sock covers a foot. Shoe is tempting, but a shoe is another piece of clothing, not a body part.
steps: Say the link: a glove is worn on (covers) a hand.
A sock is worn on a foot — so the answer is foot.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a sock goes inside a shoe, but a glove covers a hand. Ask which body part a sock covers.
mistakes.B: Step 2: wool is what a sock can be made of. The first pair is 'clothing → body part it covers'.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a drawer is where socks are kept. Keep the link 'covers this body part'.

questions.prompt: Complete the analogy: author is to book as composer is to ___.
questions.explanation: An author writes (creates) a book; a composer writes (creates) a symphony. An orchestra performs the music but is not what the composer makes.
steps: Say the link: an author is the person who creates a book.
A composer is the person who creates music, such as a symphony — so the answer is symphony.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a composer may use a piano, but an author creates a book. Find what a composer creates.
mistakes.B: Step 2: an orchestra plays the music; it is not what the composer makes. Keep 'creator → thing created'.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a conductor is another person in music, not something a composer creates.

questions.prompt: Complete the analogy: hot is to cold as ancient is to ___.
questions.explanation: Hot and cold are opposites, so you need the opposite of ancient (very old), which is modern. 'Old' is a trap — it is a synonym, not an opposite.
steps: Name the link: hot and cold are opposites.
Ancient means very old; its opposite is new or up to date — modern.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 'old' means nearly the same as ancient. The first pair are opposites, so you need the opposite of ancient.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you stayed with the temperature words. The second pair must use the word 'ancient' and its opposite.
mistakes.D: Step 2: history is linked to ancient things, but it is not the opposite of ancient.

questions.prompt: Complete the analogy: bee is to hive as ___ is to burrow.
questions.explanation: A bee lives in a hive, and a rabbit lives in a burrow. Honey is linked to the hive, but the blank must be an animal, in the same place as 'bee'.
steps: Say the link: a bee lives in a hive.
Which animal lives in a burrow? A rabbit — so the answer is rabbit.

mistakes.A: Step 2: an eagle lives in a nest high up, not in a burrow. Which animal digs and lives in a burrow?
mistakes.B: Step 2: the blank needs an animal (like 'bee'), not another home.
mistakes.D: Step 2: honey is made in a hive, so you matched it to 'hive'. The blank must be the animal that lives in a burrow.

questions.prompt:
Which pair completes the analogy?
thermometer is to temperature as ___ is to ___
questions.explanation: A thermometer is the tool that measures temperature, and scales measure weight. A clock measures time, not an alarm, so 'clock : alarm' breaks the link.
steps: Say the link: a thermometer is a tool that measures temperature.
Test each pair: scales are a tool that measure weight — only 'scale : weight' fits.

mistakes.B: Step 2: a ruler is used alongside a pencil, but it does not measure a pencil the way a thermometer measures temperature.
mistakes.C: Step 2: an alarm is something a clock does, not the amount it measures. A clock measures time.
mistakes.D: Step 2: neither word is a measuring tool. The first word must be an instrument, like the thermometer.

questions.prompt: Choose the pair that has the same relationship as PAGE : BOOK.
questions.explanation: A page is one part of a book, and a petal is one part of a flower. Paper comes from a tree, but it is made from it, not a part of it.
steps: Say the link: a page is one of the parts that make up a book.
Test each pair: a petal is one of the parts that make up a flower — so 'petal : flower'.

mistakes.A: Step 2: an author writes a novel; that is 'creator → work', not 'part → whole'.
mistakes.C: Step 2: paper is made from trees; that is 'made from', not 'one part of the whole'.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a reader uses a novel — that is a person and an object, not a part of a whole.

questions.prompt: Complete the analogy: prologue is to novel as overture is to ___.
questions.explanation: A prologue is the opening section of a novel; an overture is the opening piece of music of an opera. The orchestra plays the overture, but it is not the work it introduces.
steps: Say the link: a prologue is the introduction at the start of a novel.
An overture is the music played at the start of an opera — so the answer is opera.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a finale is the ending of a show. A prologue is the opening of a whole work, so find the whole work an overture opens.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the orchestra plays the overture, but a novel is the whole work the prologue begins.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you stayed with book words. The second pair must be about music, because an overture is music.

questions.prompt:
Which word is the odd one out?
apple, banana, carrot, cherry
questions.explanation: Apple, banana and cherry are fruits; a carrot is a vegetable. Cherry is small but still a fruit.
steps: Find a group that three words share: apple, banana and cherry are fruits.
The word left out is carrot, a vegetable.

mistakes.A: Step 2: an apple is a fruit like banana and cherry. Look for the word that is not a fruit.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a banana is a fruit, even though it is a different shape. Find the vegetable.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a cherry is small, but size is not the group. Three are fruits — which one is a vegetable?

questions.prompt:
Which word is the odd one out?
violin, cello, trumpet, harp
questions.explanation: Violin, cello and harp are string instruments; a trumpet is a brass instrument you blow. The harp looks different but still has strings.
steps: Find what three have in common: violin, cello and harp all have strings.
The trumpet has no strings (you blow into it), so it is the odd one out.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a harp is played by plucking strings, like the violin and cello. Find the instrument with no strings.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a cello is a string instrument, like a big violin. Which one is played by blowing?
mistakes.D: Step 2: the violin has strings, just like the cello and harp. Look for the brass instrument.

questions.prompt:
Which word is the odd one out?
whisper, mutter, murmur, shout
questions.explanation: Whisper, mutter and murmur are all ways of speaking quietly; to shout is to speak loudly.
steps: Find what three have in common: whisper, mutter and murmur are quiet ways of speaking.
Shout is loud, so shout is the odd one out.

mistakes.A: Step 2: to mutter is to speak quietly and unclearly, like whisper and murmur. Which word is loud?
mistakes.C: Step 2: a murmur is a soft, low sound. Look for the one way of speaking that is loud.
mistakes.D: Step 2: whispering is the quietest, but it is still quiet like the others. Find the loud word.

questions.prompt:
Which city is the odd one out?
Paris, Sydney, Tokyo, Ottawa
questions.explanation: Paris, Tokyo and Ottawa are national capitals; Sydney is not — Australia's capital is Canberra. Ottawa is less famous, but it is Canada's capital.
steps: Find what three have in common: Paris, Tokyo and Ottawa are each the capital city of their country.
Australia's capital is Canberra, not Sydney — so Sydney is the odd one out.

mistakes.A: Step 2: Ottawa is the capital city of Canada, like Paris (France) and Tokyo (Japan). Which city is not a capital?
mistakes.B: Step 2: Tokyo is the capital of Japan. Check each city: is it its country's capital?
mistakes.D: Step 2: Paris is the capital of France. Look for the city that is big but is not a capital.

questions.prompt:
Which word is the odd one out?
square, triangle, cube, rectangle
questions.explanation: Square, triangle and rectangle are flat 2D shapes; a cube is a solid 3D shape. The triangle is the trap: it has 3 sides, but it is still flat like the others.
steps: Check for a hidden group: square, triangle and rectangle are flat (2D) shapes.
A cube is a solid (3D) shape, so cube is the odd one out.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a triangle has 3 sides instead of 4, but it is still a flat shape. Which one is solid (3D)?
mistakes.B: Step 2: a square is a flat shape like the triangle and rectangle. Find the shape that has depth.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a rectangle is flat (2D). Look for the solid shape.

questions.prompt:
Which word is the odd one out?
listen, silent, tinsel, stolen
questions.explanation: Listen, silent and tinsel are made of exactly the same letters (anagrams). Stolen has an 'o' and no 'i', so it is the odd one out.
steps: Look past the meanings: write each word's letters in alphabetical order.
listen, silent and tinsel all give e-i-l-n-s-t, but stolen gives e-l-n-o-s-t — so stolen is the odd one out.

mistakes.A: Step 2: tinsel uses the letters e, i, l, n, s, t — exactly the same letters as listen. Check each word's letters.
mistakes.C: Step 2: silent has the same six letters as listen. Find the word with a different letter.
mistakes.D: Step 2: listen is made of e, i, l, n, s, t, like two of the others. Which word has an 'o'?

questions.prompt: Which word means the same as BEGIN?
questions.explanation: Begin and start mean the same thing. Finish is the opposite, so it is a trap for antonym/synonym mix-ups.
steps: Put BEGIN in a sentence: 'The show will begin at 7.'
Swap in each option: 'The show will start at 7' means the same — so start.

mistakes.A: Step 2: finish is the opposite of begin. The question asks for the same meaning.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you can try to begin something, but 'try' does not mean begin. Swap it into a sentence to test.
mistakes.D: Step 2: waiting is not starting. Put each option in 'The show will ___ at 7' to test.

questions.prompt: Which word is the opposite of GENEROUS?
questions.explanation: Generous means happy to give; stingy means unwilling to give or share, so it is the opposite. Giving is a synonym, not an antonym.
steps: Say what GENEROUS means: happy to give and share.
The opposite is unwilling to give or share — stingy.

mistakes.A: Step 2: giving means nearly the same as generous. The question asks for the opposite.
mistakes.B: Step 2: wealthy means rich. A rich person can still be generous or not — it is not the opposite.
mistakes.C: Step 2: kind is close in meaning to generous, not opposite.

questions.prompt: Which word means the same as FRAGILE?
questions.explanation: Fragile means easily broken or damaged, which is what delicate means. 'Broken' is a trap: a fragile thing is not broken yet.
steps: Say what FRAGILE means: easily broken or damaged.
Delicate also means easily damaged — so delicate.

mistakes.A: Step 2: fragile means easily broken, not already broken. A fragile vase is still in one piece.
mistakes.B: Step 2: strong is the opposite of fragile. Look for the same meaning.
mistakes.C: Step 2: weight has nothing to do with fragile. Test: 'Handle this ___ glass with care.'

questions.prompt: Which word is the opposite of EXPAND?
questions.explanation: To expand is to get bigger; to shrink is to get smaller, the opposite. Grow is a synonym, not an antonym.
steps: Say what EXPAND means: to become bigger.
The opposite is to become smaller — shrink.

mistakes.B: Step 2: stretching makes something bigger, which is close to expand, not its opposite.
mistakes.C: Step 2: grow means almost the same as expand. You need the opposite.
mistakes.D: Step 2: an explosion pushes outward — that is more like expanding. Find the word for getting smaller.

questions.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to RELUCTANT?
questions.explanation: Reluctant means not wanting to do something, which is unwilling. Eager is the opposite.
steps: Use it in a sentence: 'He was reluctant to jump into the cold pool.' — he did not want to.
The word that means 'not wanting to' is unwilling.

mistakes.B: Step 2: eager means keen to do something — that is the opposite of reluctant.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a reluctant person might arrive late, but late does not mean reluctant. Look for the feeling.
mistakes.D: Step 2: reluctant is about not wanting to do something, not about being cross.

questions.prompt:
Read the sentence:
'The witness gave a candid account of the accident.'
In this sentence, CANDID means:
questions.explanation: A candid account is honest and open, holding nothing back. 'Secretly filmed' comes from the phrase 'candid camera', which does not fit a witness's words.
steps: Look at what candid describes: the account (what the witness said).
A witness's account can be truthful and frank — candid means honest and open.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 'candid camera' means filmed without knowing, but here candid describes what the witness said. Use the sentence.
mistakes.C: Step 2: nothing in the sentence tells you how long the account was. Test each meaning in the sentence.
mistakes.D: Step 2: a confused account would be unclear; candid is a positive word about telling the truth.

questions.prompt: Which word is the opposite of SCARCE?
questions.explanation: Scarce means in short supply, so the opposite is plentiful. Rare is a synonym, and 'frightened' comes from confusing scarce with scared.
steps: Say what SCARCE means: hard to find, not enough of it.
The opposite is 'more than enough' — plentiful.

mistakes.A: Step 2: rare means nearly the same as scarce (hard to find). You need the opposite.
mistakes.B: Step 1: you read 'scarce' as 'scared'. Scarce means in short supply.
mistakes.C: Step 2: scarce things are often expensive, but that is a result, not the opposite meaning.

questions.prompt: Which single word can mean both 'to abandon someone' and 'a dry, sandy region'?
questions.explanation: Desert (DEZ-ert) is a dry, sandy region, and to desert (de-ZERT) someone is to abandon them — same spelling. Dessert, with two s's, is pudding.
steps: Find a word for the dry, sandy region: desert.
Check the other meaning: soldiers who 'desert' abandon their post — so desert fits both.

mistakes.B: Step 2: dessert (two s's) is the sweet course after dinner. Check the spelling of each meaning.
mistakes.C: Step 2: abandon fits the first meaning only. The word must fit both meanings.
mistakes.D: Step 2: an oasis is a green spot in a desert, and it does not mean 'abandon'.

questions.prompt:
Which letter comes next?
A, C, E, G, ?
questions.explanation: Each letter is 2 places after the one before (one letter is skipped), so G + 2 = I. H forgets to skip a letter.
steps: Find the gap: A → C is +2, C → E is +2, E → G is +2.
G + 2 = I (skip H), so the answer is I.

mistakes.A: Step 2: H is only one step after G. The pattern skips one letter each time.
mistakes.B: Step 2: J is three steps after G — you skipped two letters instead of one.
mistakes.C: Step 2: K is four steps after G. Count the gap again: A to C is 2 steps.

questions.prompt:
Which letter comes next?
B, E, H, K, ?
questions.explanation: The letters go up by 3 each time (B → E → H → K), so K + 3 = N. M comes from adding only 2.
steps: Find the gap: B(2) → E(5) → H(8) → K(11) is +3 each time.
K(11) + 3 = 14, which is N.

mistakes.A: Step 2: M is only 2 after K. Count the gap again: B to E is 3 steps.
mistakes.B: Step 2: O is 4 after K. The gap stays at 3 each time.
mistakes.D: Step 2: L is the very next letter after K. Keep the same +3 gap.

questions.prompt: In a code, CAT is written as DBU. How is DOG written in the same code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward (C → D, A → B, T → U), so D → E, O → P, G → H gives EPH. CNF moves the letters backwards.
steps: Compare CAT with DBU: C → D, A → B, T → U — every letter moves 1 place forward.
Do the same to DOG: D → E, O → P, G → H, giving EPH.

mistakes.B: Step 1: you moved each letter one place back. C → D shows the code moves one place forward.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you moved each letter two places. Check: C → D is only one place.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you shifted D and G but forgot to shift the middle letter O. Every letter moves.

questions.prompt:
Which letter comes next?
Z, X, U, Q, ?
questions.explanation: The letters go back 2, then 3, then 4, so next they go back 5: Q(17) − 5 = 12 = L. M comes from repeating the jump of 4.
steps: Find the gaps: Z(26) → X(24) is −2, X → U(21) is −3, U → Q(17) is −4.
The next gap is −5: 17 − 5 = 12, which is L.

mistakes.B: Step 2: you went back 4 again. The gap grows by one each time: 2, 3, 4, then 5.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you went back 6. After going back 4, the next jump back is 5.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you went back only 3. The jumps back are growing: 2, 3, 4, …

questions.prompt: In a code, every letter is moved two places forward in the alphabet (A becomes C). A word in this code is VKIGT. What is the word?
questions.explanation: To decode, move every letter two places back: V → T, K → I, I → G, G → E, T → R gives TIGER. XMKIV is what you get by coding a second time instead of decoding.
steps: To decode, do the opposite of the code: move each letter 2 places back.
V → T, K → I, I → G, G → E, T → R, so the word is TIGER.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you moved the letters forward again. To decode, undo the code: move each letter two places back.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you moved each letter back only one place. The code moved letters two places.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you decoded the first four letters but left T unchanged. T must move back two as well.

questions.prompt:
Which letter comes next?
A, B, D, G, K, ?
questions.explanation: The gaps are +1, +2, +3, +4, so the next is +5: K(11) + 5 = 16 = P. O repeats the +4 gap.
steps: Find the gaps: A→B +1, B→D +2, D→G +3, G→K +4.
Next gap is +5: K(11) + 5 = 16, which is P.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added 4 again. The gaps grow by one each time: 1, 2, 3, 4, then 5.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you added 6. After a gap of 4, the next gap is 5.
mistakes.C: Step 2: L is just one after K. The gaps are getting bigger, not smaller.

questions.prompt:
Which letter comes next?
C, Y, F, V, I, S, ?
questions.explanation: There are two series mixed together: C, F, I (+3) and Y, V, S (−3). The next letter is in the first series: I + 3 = L. P is the next letter of the second series, which comes after that.
steps: Split into two series: 1st, 3rd, 5th letters are C, F, I; 2nd, 4th, 6th are Y, V, S.
The 7th letter continues C, F, I (+3 each time): I + 3 = L.

mistakes.A: Step 2: P continues the other series (Y, V, S). The 7th letter belongs to the series C, F, I.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you added 4 to I. The series C, F, I goes up by 3.
mistakes.D: Step 2: R is just one before S — you followed the last letter instead of splitting into two series.

questions.prompt:
An animal's name is hidden across two words in this sentence:
'The cab at the corner was yellow.'
Which animal is it?
questions.explanation: Across 'cab at' you get c-a-B-A-T, which hides 'bat'. 'Cat' is tempting because 'cab' starts with c-a, but the next letter is b, not t.
steps: Join the words and read the letters in a row, ignoring the gaps.
'ca(b at)' gives b-a-t, so the hidden animal is bat.

mistakes.A: Step 2: there is a c and an a in 'cab', but no c-a-t in a row. Check the letters in order.
mistakes.B: Step 2: look for r-a-t in a row — it is not there. Read across 'cab at'.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 'yellow' ends in o-w, but there is no c just before it. The letters must be next to each other.

questions.prompt:
A body part is hidden across two words in this sentence:
'We saw a cobra in the zoo yesterday.'
Which body part is it?
questions.explanation: Across 'cobra in' you get co-BRA IN, which hides 'brain'. None of the other body parts appears as letters in a row.
steps: Join the words: wesawacobrainthezooyesterday.
Across 'cobra in' you get b-r-a-i-n, so the hidden body part is brain.

mistakes.B: Step 2: there is no c-h-i-n in a row. Check each option against the joined-up letters.
mistakes.C: Step 2: n-o-s-e is not in the sentence. Read across the end of one word into the start of the next.
mistakes.D: Step 2: there is no k in the sentence at all, so 'knee' cannot be hidden there.

questions.prompt:
A country is hidden across two words in this sentence:
'We hope rubbish is collected today.'
Which country is it?
questions.explanation: Across 'hope rubbish' you get ho-PE RU-bbish, which hides 'Peru'. The other countries do not appear as letters in a row.
steps: Join the words: wehoperubbishiscollectedtoday.
Across 'hope rubbish' you get p-e-r-u, so the hidden country is Peru.

mistakes.A: Step 2: there is a c in 'collected' but no c-h-a-d in a row. Check each option letter by letter.
mistakes.C: Step 2: c-h-i-l-e is not in the sentence. Read across the word gaps.
mistakes.D: Step 2: s-p-a-i-n does not appear. Look at where one word ends and the next begins.

questions.prompt:
A bird's name is hidden across three words in this sentence:
'Should we drive past or keep going?'
Which bird is it?
questions.explanation: Across 'past or keep' you get pa-ST OR K-eep, which hides 'stork'. It uses the end of 'past', all of 'or' and the start of 'keep'.
steps: Join the words: shouldwedrivepastorkeepgoing.
Across 'past or keep' you get s-t-o-r-k, so the hidden bird is stork.

mistakes.A: Step 2: c-r-o-w is not in the sentence. The hidden word runs across three words here.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there is an r and an o, but r-o-b-i-n is not in a row. Check the letters in order.
mistakes.C: Step 2: s-w-a-n is not there. Look across 'past or keep'.

questions.prompt:
Which word can go in front of each of these words to make four new words?
BALL, PRINT, NOTE, STEP
questions.explanation: FOOT makes football, footprint, footnote and footstep. HAND is the trap: it works for ball and print but not for note or step.
steps: Try each option in front of all four words, not just the first one.
FOOT gives football, footprint, footnote and footstep — all real words — so FOOT.

mistakes.A: Step 2: handball and handprint work, but 'handnote' and 'handstep' are not words. It must work for all four.
mistakes.B: Step 2: fingerprint works, but 'fingerball' and 'fingerstep' are not words. Test every word.
mistakes.D: Step 2: baseball works, but 'baseprint' and 'basenote' do not. Check all four.

questions.prompt:
All cats have whiskers. Tibby is a cat.
Which statement must be true?

options.B: All animals with whiskers are cats.

questions.explanation: Every cat has whiskers and Tibby is a cat, so Tibby must have whiskers. 'All animals with whiskers are cats' reverses the fact and is not proved.
steps: Put the facts together: Tibby is a cat, and every cat has whiskers.
So Tibby must have whiskers.

mistakes.A: Step 2: nothing says what colour Tibby is. Only choose what the facts prove.
mistakes.B: Step 2: this turns the first fact back to front. Dogs and seals have whiskers too.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the second fact says Tibby is a cat. Use the facts as given.

questions.prompt:
Ana is taller than Ben. Ben is taller than Cal.
Who is the shortest?
questions.explanation: The order from tallest is Ana, Ben, Cal, so Cal is shortest. Ben is in the middle.
steps: Line them up from tallest: Ana is above Ben, and Ben is above Cal.
Order: Ana, Ben, Cal — so Cal is the shortest.

mistakes.B: Step 2: Ben is taller than Cal, so Ben cannot be the shortest.
mistakes.C: Step 2: Ana is the tallest — she is taller than Ben, who is taller than Cal.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the two facts give a full order: Ana, then Ben, then Cal. It can be worked out.

questions.prompt:
Some students in Room 5 play chess. Everyone who plays chess is in the chess club.
Which statement must be true?

options.A: All students in Room 5 are in the chess club.
options.B: Everyone in the chess club is in Room 5.
options.C: No students in Room 5 play soccer.
options.D: Some students in Room 5 are in the chess club.

questions.explanation: The Room 5 students who play chess must be in the chess club, so some of Room 5 are in the club. 'All of Room 5' is too strong, because only some play chess.
steps: Follow the chess players from Room 5: every chess player is in the chess club.
So those Room 5 students are in the club — some students in Room 5 are in the chess club.

mistakes.A: Step 2: only SOME of Room 5 play chess, so you cannot say all are in the club.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the club could have members from other rooms. This reverses the facts.
mistakes.C: Step 2: soccer is never mentioned. Only choose what the facts prove.

questions.prompt:
Five friends — P, Q, R, S and T — ran a race. There were no ties.
- Q finished before R but after T.
- S finished last.
- P finished straight after R.
Who finished first?
questions.explanation: S is 5th. T, Q, R must be in that order, with P straight after R, so the order is T, Q, R, P, S and T is first. Q is second.
steps: Place S in 5th. T comes before Q, and Q before R, with P straight after R.
The only order is T, Q, R, P, S — so T finished first.

mistakes.A: Step 2: Q finished after T, so Q cannot be first.
mistakes.C: Step 2: P finished straight after R, and R was after Q, so P is near the end.
mistakes.D: Step 1: S finished last, not first. Re-read the second fact.

questions.prompt:
If it rains, the match is cancelled. The match was NOT cancelled.
Which statement must be true?

options.D: The match was cancelled for another reason.

questions.explanation: Rain always leads to cancelling, and there was no cancelling, so there was no rain. 'It was sunny' goes too far — it could have been cloudy but dry.
steps: Rain would have caused a cancellation.
There was no cancellation, so it did not rain.

mistakes.B: Step 2: if it had rained, the match would have been cancelled — but it wasn't.
mistakes.C: Step 2: it may have been cloudy or windy. The facts only prove it did not rain.

questions.prompt:
Lena, Max, Nia and Omar sit in four seats in a row, numbered 1 to 4 from the left.
- Max is in seat 1.
- Omar is not next to Max.
- Nia sits next to Lena.
- Lena is not in seat 3.
Who is in seat 3?
questions.explanation: Omar can't be in seat 2 (next to Max), and seat 3 leaves Lena and Nia apart, so Omar is in seat 4. Lena and Nia fill seats 2 and 3, and Lena is not in 3, so Nia is in seat 3.
steps: Max is in seat 1, so Omar is not in seat 2.
If Omar were in seat 3, Lena and Nia would be in seats 2 and 4 — not next to each other. So Omar is in seat 4.
Lena and Nia take seats 2 and 3, and Lena is not in seat 3 — so Nia is in seat 3.
